title: Admission of a New Partner
outcomes: Explain why a firm admits a partner and list every adjustment needed on the date of admission.
Prepare a Revaluation (Profit and Loss Adjustment) Account, and a two-part Memorandum Revaluation Account when book values are to stay unchanged.
Transfer reserves and accumulated profits or losses to the old partners in the correct ratio.
Work out the new ratio and the sacrificing ratio in every standard situation.
Infer hidden goodwill from the capital brought in and adjust it through capital accounts.

meta.exam_tip: Admission questions usually carry 10 marks: revaluation account, capital accounts and balance sheet. Ratios and goodwill are where step marks are won or lost — always show them as working notes.

concepts.title: Why a firm admits a partner — and what must be settled first
body: A firm brings in a new partner mainly for two reasons: it needs more capital, or it needs a person with skill, contacts or management ability. Legally the old partnership ends and a new one begins (reconstitution), but the firm and its business carry on.

Before the newcomer joins, the old partners must be given everything that belongs to the period before the admission: changes in the value of assets and liabilities, reserves and undistributed profits, and the goodwill they built. Only then will the profits and losses after the admission be shared fairly in the new ratio.

So an admission question always runs through the same checklist: (1) new ratio and sacrificing ratio, (2) goodwill (Unit 2), (3) revaluation of assets and liabilities, (4) reserves and accumulated profits or losses, (5) capital brought in and any capital adjustment, (6) new balance sheet.
concepts.analogy: Joining a group trip half-way: before the newcomer chips in, the group settles what was already spent and earned so far. From then on, everyone shares costs in the new proportion.
concepts.work: When a CA firm or a family business adds a partner, the accountant prepares an "admission statement" with exactly this checklist and gets every partner to sign it before the supplementary deed is executed.

concepts.title: Revaluation Account (Profit and Loss Adjustment Account)
body: Book values are usually out of date: buildings may be worth more, machines less, some debts doubtful, and some liabilities (or assets) may never have been recorded. On admission these are corrected through a Revaluation Account — also called a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account.

Debit side: every fall in an asset, every rise in a liability, and any unrecorded liability now brought in. Credit side: every rise in an asset, every fall in a liability, and any unrecorded asset now brought in.

The balance is the gain or loss that arose while only the old partners owned the business, so it goes to the OLD partners in the OLD ratio. The new partner gets nothing from it. Assets and liabilities then appear in the new balance sheet at the revised figures.

concepts.analogy: Re-pricing the shelf before a new co-owner joins: whatever the stock is really worth today belongs to the people who owned it yesterday.
concepts.work: In practice a valuer certifies the property, the accountant reviews ageing of debtors for the provision and searches for unrecorded bills. The revaluation figures are agreed in writing because they move partners' capitals directly.

concepts.title: Memorandum Revaluation Account — when book values must not change
body: Sometimes the partners agree to revalue for fairness but want the balance sheet to keep the old figures. Then a Memorandum Revaluation Account is used, in two parts.

Part I records the increases and decreases exactly as in a normal revaluation account; its balance goes to the OLD partners in the OLD ratio. Part II reverses every item of Part I; its balance (always the opposite of Part I) goes to ALL partners, including the new one, in the NEW ratio.

The asset and liability accounts themselves are not touched — only the capital accounts change. The net effect is that the new partner bears, through his capital, his share of the hidden gain (or receives his share of the hidden loss). The same result can be reached by adjusting the partners' capital accounts directly without opening any revaluation account.

head: Point
Revaluation Account
Memorandum Revaluation Account
rows: Assets and liabilities shown at revised values
Old values retained in the balance sheet
Two — Part I (changes) and Part II (reversal)
Part I: old partners, old ratio; Part II: all partners, new ratio

concepts.analogy: Pencil marks in the margin: you work out what the change would be, credit the right people, and then rub out the effect on the figures themselves.
concepts.work: Partners often prefer memorandum treatment to avoid showing a revalued building (and the questions banks ask about it). The accountant must still record the capital effect correctly, or the old partners lose part of their gain to the newcomer.

concepts.title: Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
body: General reserve, workmen-type reserves no longer needed, and a credit balance of Profit and Loss Account were all earned before the admission. They are transferred to the OLD partners' capital (or current) accounts in the OLD ratio: Reserve A/c (or P&L A/c) Dr. To Old Partners' Capital A/cs.

An accumulated loss — a debit balance of Profit and Loss Account or deferred revenue expenditure shown on the assets side — is the reverse: Old Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c, in the old ratio.

If the partners decide to keep the reserve in the books, the newcomer would otherwise get a share of something he did not earn; an adjusting entry is then passed debiting the new partner's capital with his share and crediting the old partners in their sacrificing ratio.
concepts.analogy: Savings in the family piggy bank before a cousin moves in belong to the family that saved them.
concepts.work: Auditors check that the reserve has actually been credited to the old partners before the admission date — a common slip is to leave it in the books and later distribute it in the new ratio.

concepts.title: Computing the new profit sharing ratio — five situations
body: I. Only the new partner's share is given: unless agreed otherwise, the old partners continue in their old ratio between themselves. New share of an old partner = (1 − new partner's share) × his old share.
II. The new partner takes stated fractions from each old partner: new share = old share − fraction given.
III. Each old partner surrenders a fraction OF HIS OWN share: amount surrendered = old share × that fraction; the new partner's share is the total surrendered.
IV. The new partner takes his whole share from one partner: only that partner's share is reduced.
V. The new partner takes his share from the old partners in a given ratio: each gives (new partner's share × his part of that ratio).
Always convert to a common denominator at the end and reduce the ratio to its simplest whole numbers.
concepts.analogy: A pizza already cut 5:3 between two friends. A third friend arrives — either both trim their slices in proportion, or one gives up more, or they each cut off a stated piece.
concepts.work: Ratios go into the supplementary partnership deed and into the tax computation of each partner's share. A wrong fraction here silently mis-states every year's profit distribution until someone notices.

concepts.title: Sacrificing ratio (and gaining partners)
body: Sacrifice of an old partner = old share − new share. The ratio of these sacrifices is the sacrificing ratio. It is used to credit the old partners with the new partner's share of goodwill (premium).
In situation I the sacrificing ratio equals the old ratio. In every other situation it must be worked out — never assume it.
If an old partner's new share is larger than his old share, he is a gaining partner for that change; a gain is new share − old share.
concepts.analogy: If you give up part of your slice, you are the one who should be paid for it — and in proportion to how much you gave up.
concepts.work: Premium for goodwill is a real cash receipt shared between partners. Crediting it in the old ratio instead of the sacrificing ratio is one of the most frequent errors found when reviewing admission entries.

concepts.title: Hidden goodwill
body: Sometimes no value of goodwill is stated, but the capital the newcomer brings is more than his fair share of the net worth. The difference is goodwill "hidden" in the deal.

Hidden goodwill = (new partner's capital × reciprocal of his share) − (old partners' capitals + reserves and undistributed profits + any revaluation gain − accumulated losses + new partner's capital).

The new partner's share of this goodwill is debited to his capital account and credited to the old partners in their sacrificing ratio (goodwill is not raised in the books, as only purchased goodwill may be recorded).

blocks.text: Example: X and Y have capitals of ₹50,000 each. Z brings ₹60,000 for a 1/3 share. Implied total capital = 60,000 × 3 = ₹1,80,000; actual capital = 50,000 + 50,000 + 60,000 = ₹1,60,000; hidden goodwill = ₹20,000; Z's share ₹20,000 × 1/3 = ₹6,667 (rounded).

concepts.analogy: If someone pays ₹40 for a quarter share of a box of chocolates whose contents are worth only ₹120 in all, they are paying ₹10 extra for something you cannot see — the box's reputation.
concepts.work: When a professional joins a well-known firm, the deal is often framed only as "bring ₹X for one-third". An accountant must spot the implied goodwill, or the old partners are under-credited.

illustrations.title: Admission with revaluation, reserve and premium for goodwill
illustrations.q: Arora and Bhat share profits 3:2. Their Balance Sheet at 31 March 2026: Trade payables ₹60,000; General Reserve ₹25,000; Capitals — Arora ₹1,50,000, Bhat ₹1,00,000 (total ₹3,35,000). Assets: Building ₹1,20,000; Machinery ₹80,000; Inventory ₹50,000; Trade receivables ₹55,000; Bank ₹30,000. On 1 April 2026 Chopra is admitted for a 1/4 share. She brings ₹1,20,000 as capital and ₹40,000 as premium for goodwill. Agreed: building to be valued at ₹1,44,000; machinery depreciated by 10%; inventory written down by ₹4,000; provision for doubtful debts at 5% of receivables; outstanding wages of ₹3,250 not yet recorded. Pass journal entries, prepare the Revaluation Account, Partners' Capital Accounts and the new Balance Sheet.

On 1 July 2026 Isha is admitted for a 1/4 share and brings ₹1,50,000 as capital. Nothing is said about goodwill or about the old partners' future ratio. jobs.title: Admission statement for a growing consultancy firm
jobs.role: Article assistant helping the accounts partner of a client firm
jobs.situation: A two-partner engineering consultancy is bringing in a third partner for a one-fourth share. The partners send you last year's balance sheet, a valuer's report on their office, and an e-mail saying "the newcomer brings ₹25 lakh, that covers everything".
steps: Fix the new ratio and the sacrificing ratio first — confirm in writing whether the old partners keep their old ratio between themselves.
Ask whether ₹25 lakh is only capital or also includes goodwill. If no goodwill figure is agreed, work out the hidden goodwill from the net worth.
Prepare a revaluation working: office per valuer, provision on old debtors, unrecorded expenses and any claims pending.
Transfer the general reserve and undistributed profit to the old partners in the old ratio.
Draft the capital accounts and the opening balance sheet of the new firm, and have every partner sign the statement before the supplementary deed is drafted.
jobs.takeaway: An admission is a settlement of the past before a sharing of the future; every adjustment has to be agreed in writing because it moves partners' capitals.
jobs.think: The old partners want the revalued office to stay at its old book value in the balance sheet. Which account do you use?
jobs.answer: A Memorandum Revaluation Account (or direct capital adjustments): Part I credited to old partners in the old ratio, Part II reversed among all partners in the new ratio. Book values stay unchanged.

jobs.title: Admitting a partner into an LLP
jobs.situation: An LLP is admitting a new partner who will contribute ₹10 lakh. The accounting is the same as for a firm, but there are LLP formalities too.
steps: Check what the LLP agreement says about admission, contribution, profit share and goodwill.
Record the contribution, revaluation and reserve transfers exactly as for a partnership firm.
Get the supplementary LLP agreement signed and file the prescribed notice of change in partners with the Registrar (Form 4) within 30 days.
Update the partners' contribution figures shown in the next annual filings.
jobs.takeaway: Partners' capital in an LLP is called contribution, but revaluation, reserves and goodwill on admission follow the same accounting logic as a firm.

mcqs.explain: Falls in asset values are losses — Revaluation A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c.

options: Old partners in the old ratio
All partners in the new ratio
Old partners in the sacrificing ratio
mcqs.explain: The change in values arose before the admission, so it belongs to the old partners in their old ratio.

mcqs.q: X and Y share 5:3. Z is admitted and the new ratio is 3:2:1. The sacrificing ratio of X and Y is:
In a Memorandum Revaluation Account, the balance of the second part is shared by:

Old partners in the old ratio
Old partners in the sacrificing ratio
mcqs.explain: Part II reverses Part I and its balance is shared by all partners in the new ratio, so the book values stay unchanged.

mcqs.q: General Reserve of ₹30,000 appears in the books of A and B (2:1) when C is admitted. A's capital is credited with:
mcqs.explain: Reserves go to the old partners in the old ratio: 30,000 × 2/3 = ₹20,000.

mcqs.q: A and B have capitals of ₹60,000 and ₹40,000. C brings ₹50,000 for a 1/4 share. Hidden goodwill of the firm is:
mcqs.explain: 50,000 × 4 = 2,00,000 implied capital; actual 1,50,000; hidden goodwill ₹50,000 (C's share would be ₹12,500).

An unrecorded liability discovered at the time of admission is:
options: Debited to the new partner's capital account
mcqs.explain: Bringing in a liability reduces net worth — it is a loss on revaluation (Revaluation A/c Dr. To Liability A/c).

A debit balance of Profit and Loss Account of ₹16,000 appears when C is admitted into the firm of A and B (equal partners). The entry is:

Debit Profit and Loss A/c ₹16,000; credit A, B and C equally
Debit C ₹5,333; credit Profit and Loss A/c
mcqs.explain: An accumulated loss belongs to the old partners and is written off to their capitals in the old ratio.

mcqs.explain: The old partners are compensated for the share they give up, so they are credited in the ratio of their sacrifice.

Calculate the new ratio and the sacrificing ratio in each case: (a) Kiran gets 1/6 share and nothing else is agreed; (b) Kiran gets 1/6 share, contributed equally by Jay and Kunal; (c) Jay surrenders 1/4 of his share and Kunal surrenders 1/6 of his share in Kiran's favour.

remarks: Case (c) separates good answers from average ones: the fraction surrendered is a fraction of the partner's own share, not of the whole firm.
Many candidates stop at fractions; the examiner expects the ratio reduced to whole numbers.
mistakes: Assuming the sacrificing ratio is always the old ratio.
tips: Lay the three cases out in one table — working, new ratio, sacrificing ratio.
Convert all shares to a common denominator before writing the ratio.

questions.q: Rao and Sen share profits equally. Their Balance Sheet at 30 September 2026 shows: Trade payables ₹48,000; Profit and Loss Account (credit balance) ₹18,000; Capitals — Rao ₹1,80,000, Sen ₹1,20,000 (total ₹3,66,000). Assets: Land and building ₹1,50,000; Plant ₹90,000; Inventory ₹60,000; Trade receivables ₹52,000; Bank ₹14,000. On 1 October 2026 Tara is admitted for a 1/3 share; the new ratio is equal. She brings ₹1,50,000 as capital and her share of goodwill in cash; the firm's goodwill is valued at ₹90,000. Land and building is to be increased by ₹36,000, plant reduced by 10%, a provision for doubtful debts of ₹2,400 created, and an unrecorded claim for damages of ₹1,600 is to be provided for. Prepare the Revaluation Account, the capital accounts of the partners and the new firm's Balance Sheet.

summary: Admission = reconstitution: settle the past (revaluation, reserves, goodwill) before sharing the future in the new ratio.
Revaluation Account: Dr decreases in assets and increases in liabilities; Cr increases in assets and decreases in liabilities; balance to old partners in old ratio.
Memorandum Revaluation: Part I old partners old ratio; Part II reversal, all partners new ratio; book values unchanged.
Reserves / P&L credit to old partners in old ratio; accumulated losses debited to them in old ratio.
New ratio — five situations; sacrificing ratio = old share − new share.
Hidden goodwill = new capital × reciprocal of share − (old capitals + reserves + new capital).
remember: If only the new share is given, old partners keep their old ratio and sacrifice in it.
Premium for goodwill → sacrificing ratio; revaluation and reserves → old ratio.
Unrecorded liability = loss on revaluation; unrecorded asset = gain.
traps: Don't give the new partner a share of revaluation profit or reserves.
Don't compute surrender in Case III on the whole firm — it is a fraction of the partner's own share.
Don't raise goodwill as an asset when it is only hidden in the capital brought in.

viva.q: Why are assets and liabilities revalued when a new partner is admitted, and who gets the profit or loss on revaluation?
viva.model: Book values are often out of date, so assets and liabilities are revalued to bring them to their fair value on the date of admission. The gain or loss arose while only the old partners owned the firm, so the profit or loss on revaluation is transferred to the old partners in their old profit sharing ratio. The new partner gets no share of it.

viva.q: How do you calculate the new profit sharing ratio when only the new partner's share is given?
viva.model: When only the new partner's share is given, it is assumed that the old partners continue to share among themselves in their old ratio. So I subtract the new partner's share from one, and divide the balance between the old partners in their old ratio. Each old partner's new share is the remaining share multiplied by his old share. In this case the sacrificing ratio is the same as the old ratio.

viva.model: Sacrificing ratio is the ratio in which the old partners give up their share of profit in favour of the new partner. Each partner's sacrifice is his old share minus his new share. It is used to credit the old partners with the new partner's share of goodwill or premium.

viva.q: How is a general reserve shown in the old balance sheet treated on the admission of a partner?
viva.model: The general reserve was built from profits earned before the admission, so it belongs to the old partners. It is credited to the old partners, in their old ratio, by debiting General Reserve Account and crediting their capital accounts. The new partner does not get any share of it.

viva.q: What is a Memorandum Revaluation Account and how is it different from an ordinary Revaluation Account?
viva.model: A Memorandum Revaluation Account is used when the partners want the assets and liabilities to stay at their old book values. It has two parts. The first part, which records the changes, goes to the old partners in the old ratio. The second part, which reverses the same items, is shared by every partner, the newcomer included, in the new ratio. An ordinary revaluation account has one part and the revised values appear in the balance sheet.

viva.q: How do you find hidden goodwill when the value of goodwill is not given?
viva.model: Multiply the new partner's capital by the reciprocal of his share to get the total capital the firm should have. From this deduct the actual capital, which is the old partners' capitals plus reserves and undistributed profits plus the new partner's capital. The difference is the hidden goodwill. The new partner's share of it is debited to his capital and credited to the old partners in the sacrificing ratio.

cases.title: Neel joins Mira & Om
cases.case: Mira and Om share profits equally, with capitals of ₹2,50,000 and ₹2,00,000 and a General Reserve of ₹30,000. On admitting Neel for a 1/3 share (new ratio equal), they find that land is worth ₹48,000 more than book value, machinery is overvalued by ₹12,000 and a provision for doubtful debts of ₹6,000 is required. Revised values are to be shown in the books. Neel brings ₹3,00,000 as capital; nothing is said about goodwill.

mcqs.q: What is the profit on revaluation?
mcqs.explain: 48,000 − 12,000 − 6,000 = ₹30,000, credited to Mira and Om equally.

mcqs.q: What is the hidden goodwill of the firm?
mcqs.explain: Implied capital 3,00,000 × 3 = 9,00,000. Actual = 2,50,000 + 2,00,000 + 30,000 reserve + 30,000 revaluation gain + 3,00,000 = 8,10,000. Hidden goodwill = ₹90,000. (₹1,20,000 forgets the revaluation gain; ₹1,50,000 forgets both the reserve and the revaluation gain.)

mcqs.q: How much is debited to Neel's capital account for goodwill?
mcqs.explain: Neel's 1/3 of ₹90,000 = ₹30,000, credited ₹15,000 each to Mira and Om (sacrifice 1/6 each).

mcqs.q: In what ratio is the General Reserve transferred?
options: Not transferred; it stays in the books
mcqs.explain: Reserves belong to the old partners and are credited in the old ratio (equal).
